content.thinking:
Working out the postmortem: memory has been climbing on io-shop with no deploys or flag changes, and a restart confirmed it as mitigation. I'm weighing a code reading of an unbounded module-level dict in visits.py as the cause, though nothing has actually run it, so that is still unverified. I'm also trying to pin down the user-facing symptom, where requests slowed and latency rose across the service.

I'm now laying out the causal chain, starting with requests to the shop slowing from the onset and tying that to memory climbing in the running process. A restart brought latency back, which supports the memory growth, though the link from memory to latency is still a candidate rather than shown.

I'm now going through the third causal step: no deploy or flag change set off the memory growth, so I'm checking whether an earlier revision could be ruled out. The service looked healthy before onset on the same revision, and I'm still weighing whether demand could account for the climb.

I'm checking whether the deploy and flag history actually rules anything out. No deploy turned up in the day before onset, and the only flag change in the hour before was made by Argus. The running revision isn't named in the history, so I can't treat it as cleared, and given a leak in a long-running process, the code itself is still the likely culprit.

Now I'm working out how the memory growth leads to the root cause: the reading of the visits code says each account page served adds a shopper entry to a process-wide store that is never trimmed, so a long-running process keeps growing as new shoppers arrive.

I'm settling the root cause now: the visits code adds each new shopper to a module-level store that nothing trims, so the process's memory grows with every new visitor. The rest of the postmortem fields are the cause in plain terms and the risk that memory climbs again after the restart.

I'm now getting the contributing factors down: the memory alert only fired once the climb had already run for a while, and there was no latency alert on io-shop to catch the slowdown sooner. I'm also looking at why the existing test for the visits code never flagged that its store grows without a bound.

I'm now checking the contributing factors: the postmortem probably needs a note that the alert paged nobody, since no on-call incident was linked. Paging wouldn't have shortened the response, since Argus handled it within a couple of minutes, but it's still a gap worth recording.

Now I'm listing the remaining actions: a latency alert on io-shop to catch the slowdown earlier, a check that flags module-level stores without a size bound, and routing the high-memory alert to on-call paging.

Now I'm drafting the went-well and went-wrong lessons: Argus's restart brought the service back, the Investigator ruled out deploys and flag changes, and Code-Fix put up a draft fix. The paging gap is the thing I still need to write down.

I'm settling the got-lucky and assumptions parts: the restart came before memory reached the container limit, and the claim that latency rose because of the memory growth rests on the timing and the restart, not on a measurement.

I'm checking the causal chain's evidence: latency is the symptom to tie to memory, and the metrics readings and the alert that fired give the timing. Each step needs its citations lined up, and the claim that memory grew with no change in the running process needs the deploy and config records behind it. I'm also noting that the replica-level assumption is still unchecked.

I'm checking the symptom wording against the rest of the document: requests slowing is what the metrics read showed, so I'll tie the causal chain to that and keep the replica claim to "every replica" rather than a count.

action_items.item: Add an alert on io-shop's p95 and p99 request latency compared with its usual level, so a slowdown is caught without waiting on the memory rule.
Add a review or lint check to io-shop that flags module-level dicts or caches with no size bound.
Audit io-shop for other module-level stores that add an entry per distinct shopper or user without ever removing any.
Route HighMemoryUsage on io-shop to the on-call paging policy, so a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Requests to io-shop took longer to answer from the onset onward, at the median and even more for the slowest requests.

The io-shop process's memory kept climbing toward its container limit while requests slowed. The application logged a rising heap against its limit, and the growth was confined to the running process: the restart cleared it.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or release of io-shop in the day before the onset: none was found.
A feature flag change by anyone but Argus in the hour before the investigation, a window that covers the onset: none was found.

causal_chain.step: The memory grew inside the running process with no production change to set it off. No deploy or release was found in the day before the onset, and no flag change in the hour around it. Every replica ran one revision, but the history does not name it, and the record does not show when it went out or show the service healthy after it. That revision was not ruled out.

Each account page served records the shopper in a store shared across the whole process. According to Code-Fix's reading of visits.py, that store keeps one entry for every new shopper and nothing trims it, so the process grows as new shoppers arrive.

input.cause_in_plain_words: The shop's server likely kept a note of every shopper who visited and never threw any of those notes away, so it used more and more memory the longer it ran.

contributing_factors.factor: Only the memory alert found the problem, and its rule waits for its condition to hold before it fires. No alert on io-shop's request latency was seen, even though latency rose from the onset.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: An alert on request latency could have flagged the slowdown well before the memory rule's wait ran out, which would have brought the restart sooner and shortened the slow stretch.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that catches a process-wide store with no size limit before it ships. The module's own test describes the store growing without anything removing entries, and that was not flagged.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The store would have been bounded before it reached production, and the memory growth behind the slowdown would not have built up.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent checked deploys and flag changes and found none, ruling out a recent production change before anything was tried.
The Mitigation Agent restarted io-shop for C1.
The Mitigation Agent checked the service after the restart and judged the action confirmed.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #531 for a person to review.

went_wrong: The alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.

input.root_cause: In src/io_shop/visits.py, `record_visit`, which serve_account_page calls for each account page it serves, adds an entry for every new shopper id to the module-level dict `_LAST_SEEN`, and nothing in the files Code-Fix read removes entries except `forget_every_visit`. A long-running io-shop process therefore keeps growing in memory as new shoppers arrive, even when request volume stays flat.
input.still_at_risk: As new shoppers visit, memory in the restarted io-shop could climb toward its limit again and slow requests the way it did here.
input.symptom: Requests to the shop slowed down
